title: Unlimited / uncapped liability
text: Clauses imposing unlimited or uncapped liability on a party create unbounded financial exposure and should normally be rejected. Standard market practice caps liability at one of: (a) the total contract value over the term; (b) the fees paid in the prior 12 months; (c) a fixed monetary amount such as twice the annual fees. Carve-outs from the cap are common for: gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, indemnification obligations, breach of confidentiality, breach of data protection, and IP infringement. Mutual caps are preferred; one-sided caps that protect only one party are a red flag in negotiated agreements.

title: Exclusion of indirect, consequential, and special damages
text: Standard liability clauses exclude indirect, consequential, special, incidental and punitive damages, as well as lost profits, lost revenue, loss of goodwill, and loss of data. The interpretation of 'consequential damages' varies by jurisdiction (under English law it generally means losses arising naturally from the breach beyond direct losses; under New York law it is interpreted more narrowly). Reviewers should ensure that loss of data is explicitly addressed because many courts treat it as direct rather than consequential when the contract concerns data services.

title: IP assignment and work made for hire
text: Full IP assignment or 'work made for hire' clauses transfer ownership permanently and irrevocably to the receiving party. Before signing, verify carve-outs for: pre-existing IP (background IP) owned before the engagement; tools, methodologies, and know-how developed independently and not specific to the deliverables; open-source components subject to their own licences; joint inventions and improvements. Without these carve-outs, an engineer or consultant risks assigning their entire body of work, including templates and reusable components. Joint IP ownership creates licensing complexity (each owner can typically license without the other's consent) and is usually best avoided unless deliberately intended.

title: Perpetual, irrevocable, and unlimited licences
text: Licence grants described as 'perpetual', 'irrevocable', or 'sublicensable' permanently encumber the licensor's IP. 'Perpetual' means the licence has no time limit; 'irrevocable' means the licensor cannot terminate it (even for breach in some drafting); 'sublicensable' lets the licensee further licence to third parties without limit. The combination of perpetual + irrevocable + sublicensable + exclusive is effectively a transfer of ownership without the price tag. Negotiation pattern: limit licence duration, retain termination for material breach, restrict sublicensing to affiliates only, and avoid exclusivity unless premium consideration is paid.

title: Non-compete and restrictive covenants
text: Non-compete reasonableness factors: geographic scope (worldwide bans are rarely enforceable, regional or city-level scope is the norm), duration (typically 6 to 24 months post-termination), legitimate business interest protected (confidential information, customer relationships, trade secrets), and the consideration received in exchange. Many jurisdictions limit or void overbroad non-competes: California (Business and Professions Code §16600) voids almost all employee non-competes; the US FTC's 2024 final rule attempted a nationwide ban on most worker non-competes; several EU member states require compensation for the duration of the restriction. In B2B contracts non-competes are more often enforceable but still subject to reasonableness.

title: Change of control triggers
text: Change of control clauses define what events allow termination or trigger pre-emptive rights. Acceptable variants require notice and consent (with consent not to be unreasonably withheld), or exclude internal corporate reorganisations and affiliate transfers from the trigger. Problematic variants include automatic termination on any change of beneficial ownership above a low threshold, broad anti-assignment language that captures M&A as 'assignment by operation of law', or rights of first refusal that allow the counterparty to acquire the contract. In M&A diligence these clauses are routinely identified, valued, and either consented to or negotiated as part of the closing conditions.

title: Termination for convenience
text: Termination for convenience (T4C) lets a party end the contract without cause on notice. Customer-side T4C is standard in services agreements but often paired with: a minimum notice period (30 to 90 days), payment for work performed up to the termination date, payment for non-cancellable third-party commitments, and a wind-down or transition assistance obligation. Where T4C is absent, parties are limited to termination for cause (material breach, insolvency, force majeure), which is harder to invoke. Long notice periods (six months, one year) make T4C nearly meaningless and should be flagged.

title: Auto-renewal and evergreen terms
text: Auto-renewal clauses extend the contract term unless one party gives notice of non-renewal before a specified deadline (the 'non-renewal window'). Risk factors: long notice windows (90 to 180 days) that make it easy to miss the deadline; multi-year renewal periods rather than annual; price-increase mechanics tied to renewal; absence of an exit on price increases. Many jurisdictions (California, France, several US states) restrict auto-renewal of consumer subscriptions, requiring conspicuous disclosure and easy cancellation. B2B auto-renewals are generally enforceable but reviewers should diary the non-renewal deadline immediately.

title: Governing law and sanctioned jurisdictions
text: Governing-law clauses pointing to OFAC-sanctioned countries (such as Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Syria, and certain regions of Ukraine) create enforcement risk and potential secondary-sanction exposure for third parties. Counterparties domiciled in sanctioned jurisdictions also raise screening obligations under EU and UK sanctions regimes. Standard low-risk alternatives in international commerce: English law (London arbitration), Delaware law (US deals), Swiss law (neutral European choice), Singapore law (Asia-Pacific deals). Reviewers should also check the dispute-resolution forum: a contract under English law with mandatory courts in Moscow undermines the choice of law.

title: Confidentiality and NDA scope
text: Confidentiality obligations should cover: a clear definition of confidential information (including oral disclosures if marked / confirmed in writing), permitted purposes, permitted recipients (employees, contractors, professional advisors on a need-to-know basis with equivalent obligations), standard exclusions (information already known, independently developed, received from a third party without restriction, in the public domain through no fault of the recipient, required by law to be disclosed). Duration is typically 3 to 5 years for ordinary confidential information, but indefinite for trade secrets. Residual-knowledge clauses (permitting unaided memory use) materially weaken confidentiality and should be reviewed carefully.

title: Indemnification scope and procedure
text: Indemnification clauses oblige one party to compensate the other for specified losses, typically third-party claims relating to: IP infringement, breach of confidentiality, breach of representations and warranties, gross negligence, willful misconduct, breach of laws, breach of data-protection obligations. The procedure should specify: prompt written notice (within 10 to 30 days, but lack of timely notice should not excuse the indemnifier unless materially prejudiced); right of the indemnifier to control the defence and settlement (subject to no admission of liability for the indemnified party and no non-monetary remedy without consent); cooperation by the indemnified party. Indemnification caps are increasingly common and should match the liability cap structure.

title: Data-processing addendum (DPA) essentials
text: A DPA between a controller and processor under GDPR Article 28 must address: (a) subject matter, duration, nature, and purpose of processing; (b) types of personal data and categories of data subjects; (c) processor obligations including processing only on documented instructions, confidentiality of personnel, security measures (Article 32), engagement of sub-processors only with prior authorisation, assistance with data-subject requests and Article 32-36 obligations, deletion or return of data at the end of services, audit rights for the controller. International transfers require additional safeguards (SCCs, BCRs, adequacy). The 2021 SCCs (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914) replaced the 2010 SCCs and must be used for new transfers; review existing contracts for outdated 2010 SCCs.

title: Warranties and disclaimers
text: Express warranties commonly include: title and non-infringement of IP, conformance to specifications or documentation, services performed in a professional and workmanlike manner. Implied warranties (merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose) are frequently disclaimed using 'AS IS' language; in jurisdictions where these warranties cannot be fully disclaimed (consumer transactions, some civil-law systems), the disclaimer should be expressed 'to the maximum extent permitted by law'. Warranty duration commonly matches the term of the agreement or a specified period (90 days, 1 year); 'lifetime' or 'perpetual' warranties create indefinite liability tails. Sole and exclusive remedies for warranty breach (re-performance, refund) limit damages exposure.

title: Force majeure
text: Force-majeure clauses excuse performance when caused by events beyond a party's reasonable control. Modern drafting typically lists: acts of God, war, terrorism, civil unrest, government actions, pandemics, natural disasters, cyber attacks, supply-chain failures by third parties not under the party's control. Post-COVID, explicit inclusion of 'epidemics, pandemics, and quarantine restrictions' is now standard. Important limits: payment obligations are usually excluded from force-majeure relief; the affected party must give prompt notice and mitigate; prolonged force-majeure events (typically over 60 to 180 days) often give either party termination rights. 'Hardship' provisions (where performance becomes uneconomic rather than impossible) are common in civil-law contracts but rare in common-law contracts.

title: Most-favoured-nation (MFN) clauses
text: MFN clauses require one party to extend to the counterparty pricing or terms at least as favourable as those given to any other customer. Risk factors: scope (worldwide vs. specific markets; all customers vs. specific tier); duration (the longer the MFN, the greater the constraint); types of terms covered (price only vs. price plus all commercial terms). MFN clauses can attract competition-law scrutiny because they may facilitate tacit collusion and raise prices market-wide; the European Commission and several national competition authorities have investigated and prohibited MFN clauses (especially in online distribution and digital platforms). Narrow MFNs limited to identical products and short durations are lower-risk.
